author: reek
body: AHCI (GopAhci, B3.1b) -- modern boards, q35, both machines in our matrix. Found by PCI class; the HBA fetches the sector by DMA.

author: reek
body: AHCI is tried first because a board with both usually presents the boot disk on the AHCI controller, and the legacy ports may answer for an empty compatibility channel.

author: reek
body: Wait for BSY to clear. Returns the last status byte read; the caller checks ERR. Fuel-bounded: exhaustion returns the busy status so the caller sees BSY still set and treats it as a failure.

author: reek
body: Program the count and LBA once, then drain `count` sectors, waiting for DRQ before each. Returns 1 on success.

author: reek
body: Dispatch order answers "which controller responds", not "which medium is mine" -- and on a real machine the internal SATA disk responds on AHCI before the boot stick responds on USB, so every read above this layer would come from the WRONG disk. The selection cells fix the medium by content: GopMedium probes each candidate (does its ESP carry our own CODEX.CDX?) by steering these cells and locks the winner. While the magic is present, every read and write in this chapter goes straight to the selected medium; without it, the dispatch order below stands, which is also how the probe itself reads. The magic is written LAST, so firmware residue in the cells cannot impersonate a selection.

author: reek
body: Bulk read through the selected medium when one is locked, else through whichever controller answers. AHCI is tried first and does the whole thing in one DMA; the IDE fallback chunks it; USB mass storage is last because its bring-up is the heaviest and boards present fixed disks on the other two. On a machine that booted from a USB stick with no other disk, USB is the only path that answers.

author: reek
body: Bulk write through the selected medium when one is locked, else through whichever controller answers. AHCI DMAs the whole run; IDE chunks it and issues one flush at the end; USB rides last, same order as reads -- a write must land on the same medium a read would have come from.

author: reek
body: Try the selected medium, else AHCI, then legacy IDE, then USB mass storage. `dr-via` names the controller that answered so the caller can say which path reached the disk -- on a boot screen that distinction is the difference between "we read the stick" and "we read something".

author: val
body: LBA28 READ SECTORS (command 0x20): select the drive with the top LBA nibble, program the count and 24-bit LBA, issue the command, then for each sector poll the status port until BSY clears and DRQ sets and read 256 16-bit words from the data port. Every poll loop is fuel- bounded so a missing or wedged disk fails to a status code instead of hanging; a program hosting this compiles with the pet flag anyway, like every boot-path loop.

author: val
body: One sector is 256 words of the data port, and ATA delivers them little-endian in the order the disk lays them out, which is what the string form moves them as.

author: val
body: One command per sector costs a command per sector: a 2 MB seed is ~4200 of them, and on IDE PIO each sector is 256 port reads. Both controllers take a sector count, so a bulk read asks once. AHCI carries the whole transfer in a single PRD (up to 4 MB); IDE is capped at 256 sectors per command by its 8-bit count register, so it walks the request in chunks.

author: val
body: A machine with no legacy IDE controller floats the bus: every status read answers 0xFF, which fakes BSY, DRQ, and ERR all at once. The fuel-bounded waits then time out holding 0xFF, the DRQ test passes, and the drain loop "reads" sectors of all-ones and reports success -- a phantom disk full of garbage that outranks the real one in the dispatch. All-ones is the same floating-bus signature the i8042 and LAPIC probes retire on; one status read up front retires the whole controller.

author: val
body: Writing mirrors reading: program the LBA and count once, then push each sector's 256 words to the data port, waiting for DRQ before each. After the last sector a FLUSH CACHE forces the drive to commit -- without it a write can sit in a volatile cache and a power loss loses the identity we just saved.

author: val
body: A write is not committed until the medium says so, and only the USB path has a flush primitive today. The answer is three-state on purpose: a medium we CANNOT flush must not be indistinguishable from one we did (L-BAILVALUE). 1 is flushed, 0 is no flush primitive for this medium, -1 is a flush that was issued and failed.

author: val
body: IDENTIFY DEVICE (0xEC) answers one 512-byte sector describing the drive: the model string sits at words 27-46 and the sector counts at words 60-61 (LBA28) and 100-103 (LBA48). No LBA registers to program; select the drive, issue, drain one sector. Behind the same floating-bus gate as every other IDE entry, and a DRQ that never arrives (no device on a present controller) returns zero instead of a garbage page.
